utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Call the case, please, Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. This is case number IT-98-34-T, the Prosecutor versus Naletilic and Martinovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Could we have the witness, please. Yes, Mr. Par.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. I was just about to say that we do have our witness here. We can begin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Witness. Can you hear me?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Would you please make the solemn declaration, in accordance with the paper the usher is showing to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. You may sit down, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Par.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Your Honours. Examined by Mr. Par:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Witness. Before we begin our conversation, I wish to inform you that the Chamber has granted you protective measures so that your identity will remain private. Your name, your face, and your voice will be distorted, in case we discuss matters that would disclose your identity we'll go into private session and nobody else outside the courtroom will hear anything. Before we begin, you have a sheet of paper before you with your name on it. If your name is correctly written, please just say yes.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ME
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now I would like to ask that we go into private session for a while, and the technical booth, could we please lower the ELMO?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. We'll go into the private session.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So, Witness, you are in Pocitelj now. Will you tell us briefly something about the situation. Did anyone expect any conflict with Croats was there any tension there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ME
utterances.text: In the beginning, when I arrived, I mean, there was no particular attention, but then gradually we began to hear news that some conflicts had started in Ravno and Prozor, and after that, the 9th of May in Mostar came, and then we began to feel the tension mounting in Pocitelj itself.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. We shall come back to that 9th of May. But before that 9th of May, tell me: At that time in Pocitelj, under whose command was Pocitelj? What unit was in Pocitelj at that time? Was it the HVO? Was it the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina? Who was it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ME
utterances.text: In Pocitelj itself, there were no troops, but the inhabitants, and they were Muslims in the majority, were in the HVO at the time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you say tension began to mount at the time. So tell me: Were there any attempts for the Muslims to leave the HVO? Was something going on there? How did the Muslims behave in the HVO? How did they feel there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ME
utterances.text: After the conflict in Mostar, some people came to discuss that the -- recruit the Muslims in the HVO should join the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina with all their gear and try to take some features above Pocitelj, for instance, such as Gubavica and some other places.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Right. So you say some people came to recruit some Muslims, if I may put it that way. Who were those people? Were they from the army or what?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ME
utterances.text: They were members with the army with whom I had been before, before July, when I was in Mostar. Those were people that I had fought together, my acquaintances.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Right. So now we've reached that date when that conflict between Croats and Muslims in Mostar began. Did anything happen then in Pocitelj? And how did you learn about that conflict between Croats and Muslims on the 9th of May?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ME
utterances.text: We listened to the news, and even in Pocitelj we could hear the detonations from Mostar, the sound travelling down the Neretva. So then we realised that there was a conflict in Mostar.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were there any Muslims fighting in Pocitelj at that time? Or rather, what came to pass in Pocitelj that day and the following days?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ME
utterances.text: There was no fighting, but one could feel the tension. And about the 30th, or perhaps the 1st of July, from the command in Capljina, people came and requested that all the able-bodied Muslims would not take part in the fighting to hand down their weapons because they were taken to certain localities and provided with protection and everything else, simply so as not to participate in the fighting.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And who announced that in Pocitelj? Were you invited to a meeting or what?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ME
utterances.text: We were summoned to a meeting in a hostelry facility, a rather large place, and there the commander personnel talked there with those members of the HVO still because officially they were still in the HVO and explained the situation to them, saying that in Mostar and beyond, to the north of Mostar, the fighting was going on, that many Muslims had crossed over to the army from the HVO. They did not want that to happen in Pocitelj and they wanted to put them at certain places without the weapons, where they would stay until the -- pending the end of the conflict between the Muslims and the Croats.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And was that done? Were there any incidents? Was there any fighting, resistance, or did it all develop smoothly? How did the meeting end?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ME
utterances.text: The meeting ended normally. 90 per cent of those members handed over their weapons. Some didn't. Some tried to break through to Mostar. And we, we who turned over our weapons, were put in buses, trucks, lorries, and were taken to Gabela and Dretelj.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did it involve only able-bodied men or was there somebody else there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ME
utterances.text: Yes, only able-bodied men, who were all members of the HVO. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And where were you taken?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ME
utterances.text: I was taken to Dretelj.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us something about the conditions in Dretelj? Did anything happen to you in Dretelj? How were you accommodated? Did anybody mistreat you? What was food like?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ME
utterances.text: Well, as soon as we were brought to Dretelj, we realised that we had been deceived because our belongings were taken from us, our money, our cigarettes, and we were put in hangars, about 400 metres square large, with some 600 people in them. Food, I couldn't even eat it because it was bad, and there was mistreatment of some people.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did anybody mistreat you, beat you, strike you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ME
utterances.text: After a few days they received information there was a member of the army. There were about 30 of us. We were called out and, and as of that day, mistreatment began.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did they mistreat and abuse only 30 of you? That is, those they had established had been with the army or others too?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ME
utterances.text: Only those who had been with the army. They called us "golden lilies."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you explain what does that mean, golden lilies? Why did they call you golden lilies?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ME
utterances.text: Golden lily is the high highest decoration of valor in the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Mr. Par, please keep your red light shining a little bit longer, because it's very fast for the interpreter to follow you, and you are in control of the pace.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. I will bear this in mind.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We're in Dretelj still. How long did you stay there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ME
utterances.text: 47 days.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And how is it that you left Dretelj after those 47 days? What was the reason for your transfer from Dretelj, and where were you transferred to?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ME
utterances.text: From Dretelj, I was transferred -- that is, some 22 of us, I'd say, the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina had established that we were there and they sought our exchange, so we were transferred to the Heliodrom in Mostar.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you arrived at the Heliodrom with this exchange group, did the exchange take place?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ME
utterances.text: That first evening we were told that we would be exchanged the next morning, that we should have a bath or refresh ourselves, that we would be exchange the next morning around 9.00. However, the exchange did not take place because it has not been -- it had not been agreed upon.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So for some reason, the exchange was thwarted and you remained at the Heliodrom; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ME
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, please: What were the conditions at the Heliodrom, as against Dretelj? And otherwise, accommodation and food, was there any mistreatment there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ME
utterances.text: At the Heliodrom, the conditions were much better as against Dretelj. It looked as if you had come to a mountain spa. There was no mistreatment. The food was good, I mean relatively good, considering. All told, it was better than in Dretelj.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me: Did you go from Heliodrom to work in some units?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ME
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you tell us, please, what the procedure was for you, as an inmate, to be taken to a unit to work.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ME
utterances.text: In the morning they would take us out of the rooms, the classrooms in the school, they would line us up, and then they came from various units and selected the men they wanted, according to our physical build.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ever go to work in Vinko Martinovic's unit, the unit of Stela?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ME
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you know Vinko Martinovic, Stela, from before?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ME
utterances.text: I remembered him from my childhood, because I went to school near his house. That was the primary school.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did he know you? Did he remember you? And what was his attitude toward you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ME
utterances.text: Well, he knew me by sight.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell the Court what the first day looked like when you arrived at Stela's, from the moment you were taken from Heliodrom, who took you away, who met you in the unit, what happened, what they told you? So describe the first day in Stela's unit and tell us when this might have been, what the time frame was.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ME
utterances.text: The first time I went there it was late August or perhaps early September. That was the first time I went to work in Stela's unit. I think Dinko Knezovic came to collect us, with a truck, and they took us to their headquarters. Stela was absent at the moment. We all waited for him in front of the headquarters. About an hour or an hour and a half later, Stela arrived.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How large was this group? How many of you arrived? And where was the headquarters where you were brought and where you waited?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ME
utterances.text: There were some 20 of us who were brought in front of the headquarters, and this was near the Rondo.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then Stela arrived. Can you tell us in brief how he treated you, whether anything was said, whether he issued orders, whether he gave you assignments?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ME
utterances.text: We were all standing there waiting for him. He looked at us to see who we were and then he came up to me and said, "What are you doing here?" I shrugged my shoulders, and he told me to sit to one side. He asked me if I had any cigarettes. And then he took some cigarettes from a soldier and gave me a cigarette and also a cup of coffee. Then he asked his men if they needed someone, someone to take --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. That's how he addressed you. Did he talk to any of the other men in that group?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ME
utterances.text: Oh, it was a normal conversation. He asked them what was going on. But there was nothing special.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So he offered you coffee and a cigarette. Did he say anything else? Did he give you an assignment? What did you do the first day?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ME
utterances.text: The first day I did nothing. He didn't give me an assignment at all. He sat with me and we talked, and I explained how I had ended up in camp. We spent the whole day talking, sitting there in front of the headquarters. Some lads were fixing a car, others were washing it, and so on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And on that first day, did you go back to the Heliodrom? Did you see anyone else you knew in that unit?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ME
utterances.text: At about 3.00 a school friend of mine passed by. He was not a member of Stela's unit, and he was in fact a neighbour of mine. He lived in the same building as my parents. I asked him to tell my parents where I was, because they had no information about me. They didn't know what had happened.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know whether that soldier informed your parents of this and whether they received the information that you were with Stela?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ME
utterances.text: Yes, because at about 6.00, my parents came to the headquarters, just as we were being put on a truck to be taken back to the Heliodrom.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you were to go back to the Heliodrom. You were on a truck. And then your parents arrived. Did you manage to talk to them? Can you describe that event for us?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ME
utterances.text: Yes. I asked for the truck to stop and I got off and approached my parents. We talked for about ten minutes and then Stela came out and said I should get back on the truck, and he promised my parents that the next day I would come home.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So he said that you would be able to talk to them tomorrow in the house, and is that how things happened? Did Stela keep his word? Did he make it possible for you to see your parents?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ME
utterances.text: On the following morning, it was mostly the same men who came, and they took us there, and he told the driver, Dinko, to take me to my flat in a jeep. And he said he would pick me up at a quarter to 6.00 p.m. In the same place to take me back to the Heliodrom.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did you spend that whole day, up to 6.00 p.m., with your parents in their home had, and did you go back to the Heliodrom that same evening?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ME
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us: In the period of time that followed, did you go to Stela's unit every day, and were you sent to his unit as a prisoner every day?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ME
utterances.text: Yes, except for twice, when they came to the Heliodrom at night. On one occasion it was to go to work in Bijelo Polje, and on the other occasion in Santiceva Street.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the rest of the time you went to Stela's unit. How long did that go on, from the first time you went to work in Stela's unit until your release, how much time elapsed? How much time were you in Stela's unit every day?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ME
utterances.text: It was from late September, approximately, until the 4th of December, when I was released and when I went to Croatia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So for about three months you went to Stela's unit regularly. Can you explain to us now how it came about that you were constantly sent to Stela's unit? What was the system? How did it happen that you were always taken to Stela's unit?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ME
utterances.text: Mostly Stela took the same men, because his soldiers had people they knew among the prisoners, and each of them wanted to protect someone. They all had someone they wanted to protect. So they didn't have to go to other units to work. At first it was Dinko Knezovic who came to pick up the prisoners. Later it was someone else. But they always asked for the same men.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what was the explanation? For example, Dinko would arrive and perhaps they asked him, "Why are you always asking for the same men?" How could he explain that he always asked for the same men to go to Stela's unit?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ME
utterances.text: Well, Stela said we were doing special jobs and that we were already used to them, that we knew how to do them, so it was better to have the same men coming all the time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You say it was the same group of prisoners. Did they want to go to Stela's or was it something that they didn't want but had to do?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ME
utterances.text: The prisoners wanted to go. I had a conflict with Dinko, and for a few days he didn't take me there, and then I asked another prisoner to tell Stela that Dinko wouldn't take me there, and then the following day I was sent there to work again.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That was the situation with you, but how about the others? Do you know that they volunteered to go to Stela's unit, and if so, why?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ME
utterances.text: Yes, they all went there voluntarily, because that's where they felt the safest. Each of them had someone they knew that who would protect them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me: Did you sometimes spend the night there without going back to the Heliodrom at all? Did you sometimes sleep in that unit?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ME
utterances.text: To begin with, it was for one or two nights, and then we would go back for a day, and so on. In late September I stopped going back to Heliodrom at all.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The person, Dinko, or whoever it was, who collected the prisoners, how would he deal with that if you spent days and days in the same unit? What did he say to the people in the Heliodrom?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ME
utterances.text: Well, Dinko would say that we were working at night on the front line. He would say that we had special jobs to do on the front line, at night, and he didn't take us all back. He would leave a few of us and let us sleep in the headquarters.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what did you actually do at night in that unit, you if you were on your own, and whoever else was with you, what did you do in the unit throughout the night, if anything?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ME
utterances.text: Mostly we sat there in front of the headquarters, played cards, read the newspapers, and just sat there doing nothing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where did you sleep in the unit? What were the conditions there when you slept there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ME
utterances.text: On the first floor of the headquarters there were three rooms with sofas and settees and couches. We had furniture there and we had blankets to cover ourselves with.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How about hygiene? Was there water? Was there a toilet?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ME
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you guard? When you spent the nights there, were you locked in? Were there guards watching over you to prevent you escaping or perhaps committing some act of sabotage?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ME
utterances.text: There was always someone on duty in the headquarters, and we would sit there chatting with him until we went to bed, but it wasn't someone who was specially there to guard us.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say "us," how many of you would spend time there, sleep there, and who were there as prisoners but in fact did not go back to the Heliodrom?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ME
utterances.text: Well, between five and ten. There were some who would ask to go to Heliodrom in the evening in order to take some food to their friends or relatives there, or some clothes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Speaking of food, how come there was enough food there for prisoners to take food to other prisoners? Where did you eat?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ME
utterances.text: We who stayed there, we ate in the same place as Stela's unit, but the food we took back, those were mainly tins which we asked for and they gave us.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You say you ate in a place called Hladovina. Was that a restaurant or a canteen, and where was it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ME
utterances.text: Hladovina is a restaurant between the headquarters and the Rondo.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was food cooked for soldiers and prisoners there, and did you eat the same food?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ME
utterances.text: Food was cooked there for soldiers for Stela's unit, and we had the same food they did. We even ate at the same time as them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you have cigarettes? Did you have coffee? Did you have everything that the soldiers had? What did the soldiers have that you did not have, as for food or other necessities?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ME
utterances.text: We had the same food. And as for drink, there was a young man in Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. the headquarters who made coffee. He was also a prisoner. Whenever we wanted, he made coffee or tea. There was milk. And the cigarettes came from other units. There were several good mechanics in this unit who could repair cars. And Stela always made them pay -- made people whose cars were repaired pay for the services we performed, and then we used that money to buy cigarettes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You want to say that if you performed a favour for someone or did a job for them, you would be paid in some way, with money or cigarettes, and that this was at Stela's order?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ME
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let's talk a little more about the conditions in the unit. You told us that you were taken to see your parents by Dinko. Were there other occasions when you could go to your house, to your parents', and how did this happen?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ME
utterances.text: Whenever I wanted to, I asked Stela to drive me, or he would tell one of his soldiers to give me a lift. Three for four times it was he who give me a lift. Once we went to his parents' house for lunch and then he took me to my parents and I stayed there three or four hours. And I was always told to wait there for him, because I wasn't allowed to move around.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you saying that on one occasion Stela took you to lunch at his parents' home? Did I understand you well?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ME
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, this is what happened to you. What about the other prisoners who were there? Were they able to go to their homes, visit their families, change, have a bath, or were you specially privileged in this regard?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ME
utterances.text: The others who had relatives could go. Somebody would always take them. Vlado Fink was there, also a high ranking officer of the Bosnian Army, and he went to see his wife and family every day.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So the only condition was that someone should take them there and then bring them back?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ME
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During those few months that you spent in that unit, did you ever go to work at the front line, at the demarcation line on the Bulevar? Were you ever taken there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ME
utterances.text: Only once. I wasn't taken there. There was a man who was at the line, and I wanted to talk to him. And there was a soldier taking food there, and I asked if I could go with him so I could see my friend.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What about the other prisoners? Did they go to the demarcation line or to the health centre? Do you know that? Did you see that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ME
utterances.text: Only those who had someone they knew in the shift, someone they knew, because the idea was that they would go to work if they had soldiers who knew them to protect them there. So they went to the health centre in that way.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let's clarify this: Everyone had someone they knew. For example, a certain soldier would ask for a certain prisoner. Did he ask for his prisoner because he wanted to have someone to work for him or because it was a friend he wanted to look after and make sure that nobody did anything bad to him?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ME
utterances.text: It was mostly friends. They always asked for their friends.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: It's too leading and instructive, to get a ready response from the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Par, rephrase your question, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, can you explain to us what you meant when you said everyone had someone they knew, and that's why they took them to the demarcation line? What did you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ME
utterances.text: If a soldier knew the prisoners who were brought to work, he would always take the prisoner he knew to work for him so that he would protect him, not because he wanted him to work for him, because there wasn't much to do anyway.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And how would he protect him if he was taking him to the demarcation line? So, for example, I'm a soldier, I've brought my friend to the demarcation line. How would I protect him? Can you explain that to us? What did they do there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ME
utterances.text: They mostly sat in cellars, protected by sandbags. Because the demarcation line had been established long before and there was no longer any need to fortify it. So they would just sit there together and chat. And it was only those who wanted to that went to the demarcation line.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During the time you spent in the unit, did you see anyone wounded or killed during your stay there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ME
utterances.text: I remember only one occasion. I don't know what the date was - when the headquarters was shelled. One of Stela's soldiers and one of the prisoners were wounded. Stela put them in his jeep. He told us to go to the basement and he drove them to hospital in his jeep. One was wounded in the stomach and the other in the kidneys. I think his soldier was wounded in the kidneys and the prisoner was wounded in the stomach.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know the name of that prisoner? And if you do, I will ask for us to go into private session while you say the name. Do you know the name?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ME
utterances.text: No. I know his nickname, but I don't know his name exactly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And where did this happen? Was it near the headquarters? Was it at the demarcation line?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ME
utterances.text: It was in the yard of the headquarters.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was it shrapnel that they were wounded with?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ME
utterances.text: Well, the headquarters was often shelled. A shell landed some ten metres away from the headquarters, and they were wounded by shrapnel.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When shelling or shooting started, did you take shelter somewhere? Were you able to take shelter? What would happen if there was suddenly shooting while you were there in front of the headquarters? How was this organised?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ME
utterances.text: We always took shelter in the basement of the headquarters. There was a big basement down the entire length and width of the building, and that's where we all took shelter.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was the shelter the same for you and for the soldiers or were any priorities set up?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ME
utterances.text: There were no priorities. We always ran into the basement all together.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. According to what you have told us, you had good conditions, freedom of movement, you could visit your parents. Why didn't you try to escape? Did you have an opportunity to escape? You were a prisoner of war. Why didn't you try to escape, if you didn't?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ME
utterances.text: Well, I couldn't escape because, first of all, I had no documents, and I felt safest with Stela because no one could mistreat me there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you wish to leave this situation, to rejoin your wife and children? Did you have plans of that kind?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ME
utterances.text: Yes. I even talked to Stela, and he said to me -- he told me I shouldn't worry, that he guaranteed that I would be released, that he did not have the power to take me out of Mostar then, but as soon as an opportunity presented itself, he would take me out of Mostar.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you had an agreement about this, and did anything ever come of that, on the basis of his promise that he would help you, did you undertake any activities? Tell me first of all: Did you manage to leave? And then tell us, in brief, how this came about.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ME
utterances.text: On the 4th of December, I did manage to leave, but before that, Stela took me to a house belonging to a soldier of his, which is right next to the house of Stela's parents. And I spent some 15 or 20 days there. Stela organised for my parents to visit me. He or his parents -- he or one of his soldiers would bring them to me. He brought me video cassettes so I wouldn't be bored. And in the end, word got around that I was hiding there, and there were people from Central Bosnia there, from other units. And then he gave me an automatic weapon in case anyone should try to break in after dark. He said, "If they try to break in, just shoot and then one of my soldiers will come to the rescue."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So he takes you out of the unit, puts you up in a house and even gives you a weapon to defend yourself. So you're there, and whilst you are there in that house, is there any plan being made to have somebody to fetch you? Are some documents being prepared? What is being done in that regard? Do you have any idea where you will go once you are allowed to go? Can you explain it to us?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ME
utterances.text: The first solution we talked about was to leave in a cistern, in a tanker going to fetch fuel, with one of the soldiers who was in Stela's unit, but then I requested to establish contact with my brother, who was in Sweden, so that he could perhaps try to organise for me departure from Mostar. So we went and called, and my brother called a high-ranking officer in the Croatian army whom had he knew personally, asked to do us this service, this favour, and he promised he would come as soon as he found time to do that. However, meanwhile, Stela --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say an officer in the Croatian army, does that mean Croatian Amy Croatia? And where did this man live at the time? Where did your brother locate him?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ME
utterances.text: This man is a high-ranking officer in the Croatian Army and he worked in the barracks in Pula. Because after I reached Croatia, I spent a night in Pula, precisely in this barracks where the Croatian army were put up.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I interrupted you. You said that your brother called that officer, that he said to him -- that he said that he would help. So did he? And when did you leave? How? When?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ME
utterances.text: Stela organised some papers to be made for me, that I was not an HVO soldier, that there was no need for me to be in the HVO, and that I was not a military conscript, and then requested SIS to issue me with a paper that I was being released. And the SIS issued that certificate even though they said they were not supposed to do that, because they had information that I was a member of the army. And he said, "Right. But this certificate doesn't matter. It doesn't really carry much weight but it will help me in those early moments so that I can get out."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So this was a kind of a paper which regulated your status.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ME
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did this man from Croatia come to fetch you and did he take you out of Mostar?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ME
utterances.text: Yes, he did. He came in the morning. It was pretty sudden. He called my parents and then my father went to Stela and together they came to where I was because that man didn't have much time. We merely greeted one another in front of the base. We said goodbye to Stela and the other soldiers that I knew and took a car and set off to Croatia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then through Croatia to third countries, where you were regulating all those papers for a third country where did you go, if it's not a secret?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ME
utterances.text: I spent the first night with my parents -- with the parents of this gentleman who had come to me, that was in Zivogosce, the second night I spent in Pula and then in Zagreb, without any papers. But then this man told me, "Well, if necessary, I can always communicate with him," but then I reported to the Bosnian consulate in Zagreb and I was issued with a passport.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you managed to go to a third country and that country is --?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ME
utterances.text: Yes. After that I left. I think it was January sometime or late December perhaps. I went to Germany.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you -- ever reunite with your family. Where and when?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ME
utterances.text: I was reunited with my family in late 1994, early 1995, in Germany.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. So now we've seen the road you covered as a prisoner. But I'd like to approach it from a different angle. So let me go back to the unit when you were there for this couple of months at Stela's. Did you see Stela or his men persecute Muslims at the time? Did you see them engage in some other activities apart from manning the front line?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ME
utterances.text: As for the persecution, I did not see any. All I know is that some individuals came and asked Stela if he could transfer somebody across his section of the front line -- of his line of responsibility on the Bulevar, and I know of a case when a man came. I think that before, before the war he was with the JNA, an officer in the JNA. And then there was somebody to see it on his behalf, that Stela lets him across, that his section of the front line. . And he asked, "What can I take with me?" And Stela told me -- told him to take four bags, four bags of anything that he can carry. And then they called by Motorola the other side to prevent any shooting, because their man was crossing over.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did that man pay something to Stela? What kind of a deal was it? Was it just a request, the man who wanted to cross over?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ME
utterances.text: No. It was just a request, and somebody interceded on behalf of Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. that man from some other unit.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So then how does Stela organise it right? This man has come. Can I get across? Does he know that man across. What does he tell him? How did do they talk, was it a personal contact? What is it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ME
utterances.text: Well, usually, as a rule, one of Stela's men would take the man to the separation line, then they would call by Motorola people across the line. Because across the line were again people who lived all together and they knew everybody and the lines were so close together they could even shout to each other, not even needing a Motorola. So somebody would announce, "Your man is coming over. Don't fire." And this was usually done in daytime, because at night there was more fire, so it wasn't all that convenient.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. And I suppose you saw how others treated Muslims. Did any other people come there to complain to Stela, to ask him for help, people from his neighbourhood, from his locality? Those were Muslims. Did you ever see anything like that? And how were they treated?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ME
utterances.text: I know that in Stela's area of responsibility, the largest part remained in Mostar. Yes, they used to come and ask mostly for food. And later on I had a story that Stela's men spent most the food of all the HVO units. To my family, after I departed to Germany, my family received a parcel of food every week.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you know if he also helped with food, other Muslim families at the time of shortages?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ME
utterances.text: Yes, certainly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We are coming to the end of our conversation. So tell us: When and how did you find out about the charges being brought against Vinko Martinovic? And can you tell the Court: What was your reaction to that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ME
utterances.text: I returned in late 1997, or in early 1998, to Bosnia-Herzegovina. I think it was 1998 sometime that I learned that The Hague Tribunal had issued an arrest warrant for Stela, but I believe he had already surrendered by that time. Then I called our friend, a former soldier, a lad who was my school fellow, Dragan Vlaho, and he said he had placed himself at -- that I should make myself available, that if I was ready to help any with my statement, that I should make myself available.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did you mean by that? What did it mean? How? Make yourself available for what? How?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ME
utterances.text: Well, that I would be ready to testify and tell my story, to say what happened to me at the time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So that is the reason why you are here. And if I haven't offered you the opportunity to tell your story, you are -- feel free to add something, but I've finished. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ME
utterances.text: I wish to thank you very much, and what I want to add is that Stela personally saved my life, because a member of the BH army, I guess I would have fared much worse had it not been for Stela.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Witness. Thank you, Your Honours. I have finished.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Four minutes before recess. So we'll make our break here, and after the break, the Prosecution will conduct cross-examination. We'll resume at 4.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. Cross-examination, Mr. Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Your Honour, I would ask to go into private session for some time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, we'll go to the private session, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And were any of your next-of-kin arrested in Mostar at that time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ME
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you were taken to Dretelj camp; right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ME
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And who was in charge of Dretelj camp?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ME
utterances.text: The Dretelj camp belonged to the HVO. I know that its administrator was someone whose nickname was Boko. That's what people called him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was it military police or regular HVO unit?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ME
utterances.text: The military police guarded the camp, and in the camp itself there were members of the HVO, including those of Muslim origin who had stayed on with the HVO. For instance, the warehouse that we were in, it was run by a man of Muslim ethnicity.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what about prisoners? Were all of them of Muslim nationality?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ME
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, is it your testimony that somewhere around 30 of you were former ABiH soldiers? Right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ME
utterances.text: In the warehouse, where I was detained, there were about 15 of us. However, there were two or three other warehouses, and then they collected us all in one place in the warehouse where I was, and there were 30 of us there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you mean that the rest of the prisoners were civilians?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ME
utterances.text: No. Before their arrest, they had also been members of the HVO.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And who was it who mistreated you? Military police or regular HVO soldiers?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ME
utterances.text: They were regular soldiers, and I know that in the beginning it was the units from Ljubuski - I don't know the name of the unit - who mostly mistreated us. Later on there were people from Bugojno, units from Bugojno, who had been driven out by the army.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, did you ever see representatives of the Red Cross, or rather, international humanitarian organisations in Dretelj Camp?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ME
utterances.text: While I was in the Dretelj camp, no.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So let's move now to Mostar. Is it correct, Witness, that most of prisoners at Heliodrom, male prisoners, were taken to perform some sort of labour outside of Heliodrom?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ME
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know to what locations they were taken to perform job?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ME
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please, could you just inform the Trial Chamber what you know about the locations.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ME
utterances.text: These were Carina, Santiceva, Bijelo Polje; Buna; Bulevar; the old high school, Plover [phoen]; then just below the Catholic church where the 4th Battalion was; then Rodoc.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know what kind of job they performed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ME
utterances.text: For the most part, it was fortifying the lines.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did they volunteer to do this job, to the best of your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ME
utterances.text: First of all, they did not volunteer, but quite a few of them, even people who -- mostly people who were from Mostar went voluntarily because they hoped to come across someone they knew to bring them food or cigarettes to bring back to the camp.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you were taken from Heliodrom to perform some job, to Vinko Martinovic unit. Do you know what kind of unit was it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ME
utterances.text: It was called ATG Mrmak. That was a unit composed mostly of Stela's friends, people who knew him from before the war and who had been in the HOS with him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know who was Vinko Martinovic commander?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ME
utterances.text: I think it was -- well, the town had its own HVO Supreme Command which issued orders.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How do you know that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ME
utterances.text: Mostly it was the military police who arrived. When there were some talks in the headquarters, it was a van from the military police that would arrive, and then some high-ranking HVO officers would go there, whom I knew by sight, and I assume they issued orders or something like that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: For example, which high-ranking officers were there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ME
utterances.text: I wouldn't know their names, but I knew them by sight. I knew they came from Mostar.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you have any idea what position they occupied at the time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ME
utterances.text: Probably high-ranking positions, because they had their own drivers and escort.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what kind of actions did the unit perform after those visits? Could you tell the Trial Chamber?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ME
utterances.text: Well, there weren't any particular operations conducted by Stela's men except perhaps at the front line, but I never went there. So I never knew what they discussed in the headquarters. The situation was always normal. We sat there. And there were complaints made to Stela that he was treating us too softly, that he was soft on us.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who complained about that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ME
utterances.text: It was mostly those men. On one occasion word got round that Stela was letting his prisoners go home, so at the Heliodrom they banned him from taking prisoners away for a time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When was it? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ME
utterances.text: It was in the period when I used to go there. It would be August or September. For a few days they wouldn't let him take prisoners, but then they let him do it again.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What kind of uniform did Stela's soldiers wear?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ME
utterances.text: Camouflage uniforms with HVO insignia. Some had green uniforms, but most of them had camouflage uniforms, and they even had insignia saying "Mrmak."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see Mr. Vinko Martinovic wear a uniform, military uniform?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ME
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did he have any specific patches testifying to the fact that he has a military rank?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ME
utterances.text: He had no rank on his uniform. His insignia was the same as those of other soldiers, HVO had, and sometimes he even wore civilian clothes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you know any of Stela's soldiers?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ME
utterances.text: Yes, most of them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you know Ernest Takac?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ME
utterances.text: I met him when I went for work in Stela's unit. I didn't know him before that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But was he in position -- I mean, August/September, when you were performing job in Stela's unit?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ME
utterances.text: I didn't understand your question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. I will try to clarify. So you just told the Trial Chamber that you saw Takac when you were performing job in Stela's unit; right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ME
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what was Takac at that time? What his position was.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ME
utterances.text: He was a soldier, a member of the ATG Mrmak.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was he a sort of boss for the rest of the soldiers?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ME
utterances.text: I don't believe so, because with Stela you never knew who was a boss and who was a soldier.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And who were bosses in his unit, apart from Stela himself?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ME
utterances.text: Only Stela.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you know Solaja?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ME
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Samir Bosnjic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ME
utterances.text: Yes. I knew him while he was still in the HOS. He was wounded in the HOS. He had a severe head wound.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Dubravko Pehar?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ME
utterances.text: Yes. I knew him from childhood.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mladen Colak?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ME
utterances.text: Yes. I met him only when I came to Stela's unit.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it correct that he was in charge of the confrontation line?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ME
utterances.text: Are you referring to Mladen Colak?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, exactly.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ME
utterances.text: I don't know who was in charge of the confrontation line, but I do know that he did go to the line, he and Dubravko.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Dubravko Pehar?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ME
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, am I fair to say that many of Stela's soldiers were criminal offenders, already wanted by the police before the outbreak of hostilities?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ME
utterances.text: I wouldn't know about that, because I was living in Sarajevo, so I didn't know who was a criminal in Mostar.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it correct that normally they took you to Stela's unit in a group of from 15 to 30 prisoners?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ME
utterances.text: I don't know that there were ever 30. Mostly it was between 15 and 20. Sometimes the person who came to collect us would take more men without Stela's knowledge to begin with.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it correct that it was mostly Dinko Knezovic who took you from Heliodrom to Vinko Skrobo unit?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ME
utterances.text: In the beginning, yes, until Stela punished him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And who was in charge of distribution of job among prisoners?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ME
utterances.text: Well, there wasn't much to do. The group I was in, at least, we mostly stayed at the headquarters, and as I said, we fixed cars and did things of that kind. It was always the prisoners that a soldier asked for who went to the line, and those were people whom the soldiers knew. But there was never any strict distribution of jobs. They never said, "You go there" and, "You do this and that."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, is it correct to say that from those 20, 15, or 30 prisoners taken from Heliodrom, not all were left at headquarters; some were taken to the confrontation line or some other types of job? Right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ME
utterances.text: No. They weren't all left at the headquarters. That's correct. Some went home right away. Others were on lists of people taken from the Heliodrom who never even arrived in Stela's headquarters.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I repeat my question: Were any of prisoners taken to the confrontation line from your group of prisoners?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ME
utterances.text: Yes, but only those whose friends were doing their shift at the confrontation line as soldiers. Had Stela been at the confrontation line at the time, I would probably have been taken there too.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was it a lighter job and less dangerous on the confrontation line?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ME
utterances.text: It was always safest in Stela's headquarters, and that was the safest place to go to work. In the period of time I was there, the civilian protection had already set up the confrontation line, so there was not much to do, either on the lines or in the headquarters.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, how do you know that if you never go to the confrontation line, according to your testimony?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ME
utterances.text: I said that once I spent ten minutes at the confrontation line, when we went to take some food there, and I wanted to ask Dubi, that's Dubravko Pehar, about some things.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what kind of information did you get for those ten minutes that you were on the confrontation line?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ME
utterances.text: The information I got was that I could stay in Dubravko Pehar's house until I managed to leave Mostar.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it correct, Witness, that prisoners would call Stela "colonel" or "boss" or something like that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ME
utterances.text: We called him that jokingly. We also called him other names as a joke, but he didn't have any official rank, as far as I knew. He was the leader of his crew, of his people, who respected him. When the Serbian aggression started, he was one of the first to organise defence, and that's why people respected him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, how did Mr. Martinovic introduce himself to prisoners?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ME
utterances.text: He behaved normally, as the commander of his unit, but he always treated everyone correctly. And there were always jokes bandied around. The atmosphere was always relaxed. Because when you've been in a camp like Dretelj and after that you come to Stela, that was really wonderful. It was so relaxed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, is it correct that on many occasions Vinko Martinovic referred to prisoners as fundamentalists, extremists, balijas, and so on?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ME
utterances.text: No. It could only happen if he meant it as a joke, but he didn't really mean it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How do you know what he meant?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ME
utterances.text: I know because I had enough courage to call him an extremist, and he would call me a fundamentalist, but we were both joking. Because he wanted us to relax, at least a little.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, is it correct that you were not only taken to Stela's unit, but on some occasions you were taken to some other jobs?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ME
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it correct that on one occasion you were taken to the 1st Light Assault Platoon?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ME
utterances.text: I don't know the exact name of that platoon, but if you tell me the location, I can tell you if I was there or not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But what kind of job did you perform? And was it Dinko Knezovic who took you there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ME
utterances.text: Dinko Knezovic took me only to Stela's headquarters.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: I would like the witness to be shown Exhibit 567.1.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I would like you to open the page with the last four digits 5080 and 5081. Okay. Page with the digits 5081. Witness, do you see your name in the list of prisoners?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ME
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you also see Dinko Knezovic's name at the bottom of the page?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ME
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you see the name of the unit at the top of the page?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ME
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what is the name of the unit?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ME
utterances.text: The 1st Light Brigade -- assault.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You were taken there by Knezovic; right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ME
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what kind of job did you perform in that unit?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ME
utterances.text: These were all men who came to Stela's headquarters.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But what were you doing in the 1st Battalion?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ME
utterances.text: Probably they called Stela's brigade the 1st Light Assault, but that's a mistake, because we went to the Mrmak anti-terrorist group. Vladimir Fink was a high-ranking officer of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Zlatko was a tradesman. He repaired things. These were people who came to the anti-terrorist group every day, and we certainly didn't go any further than the headquarters.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, you've just explained to the Trial Chamber that on certain occasions prisoners were kept in Stela's headquarters for some time after they were brought there from Heliodrom; is it correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ME
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it correct that apart from the top floor, there was a basement in his headquarters?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ME
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it also correct that that basement was also used for keeping prisoners?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ME
utterances.text: No. Only in case of shelling. I'm sure that prisoners were never kept there unless there was shelling.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were there any occasions when prisoners were kept at Stela's headquarters for a long period of time, for example, for ten days?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ME
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you expand a little bit on that? When did it happen, and why?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ME
utterances.text: Mostly it was the men whom Stela knew most, who knew best, or whom he liked best who remained in the headquarters, and we were practically free there. We would stay the night or we would go to the Hladovina restaurant in the evening. We would sit and play cards with the soldier who was on duty. That's how it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Now I would like the witness to be shown Exhibit -- one moment. Sorry -- yes. 601.1. This is pages with the last four digits 5272, 5273.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please, Witness, take a look at the list of persons you have on this document. Witness, have you read it?

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Your Honour, maybe we should now go into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. We'll go to the private session, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, let's return to the events of the 17th of September, 1993, when some military operation took place. You were not taken on the 17th of September to Stela's unit; right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ME
utterances.text: I think that by that time I could have already been in the flat, because the only date that means something to me is December 4th, 1993. Otherwise ...

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, let's return to your testimony. You explained to the Trial Chamber that you were released from Heliodrom on the 3rd of December or 4th of December, but 15 or 20 days before, you were taken to some apartment; right? So it could not be September.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ME
utterances.text: Fifteen to twenty days before that I spent in the flat, that is correct, and on the 4th of December I left Mostar. But in the meantime, I didn't spend all this time in the flat on the 4th of December. I even could report -- could go to the base and report to Stela in order to get that paper.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, in September you were kept in Heliodrom; right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ME
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the 17th of September you were not taken to Stela's headquarters; right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ME
utterances.text: I don't remember the dates when I was taken and when I wasn't.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Some minutes ago we looked through this document and you were not in the list of prisoners taken to Stela's headquarters. Take a look at it again.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ME
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What do you mean by "yes"?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ME
utterances.text: I am not on the list. I am not on the list of people taken away.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Don't you think that it's not a coincidence?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, Mr. Par.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I object to this question. I think it invites speculation. "Was it by coincidence or not?" That is really not a question that I think is permissible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Prosecutor, you may put your question another way.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, did you consider yourself to have been a privileged prisoner?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ME
utterances.text: By the very fact that I went to Stela's, yes, but I can explain the next question. At some moment it -- that Stela was taken his prisoners home. Dinko Knezovic sometimes took out more men than Stela had asked for, and then he struck private deals to take away those people. Before he would take them to the base, he would take them to their homes and then seek payment for that. And then he would bring to the base the number of men, the exact number that Stela had asked. And these stories started to circulate around the Heliodrom, and then we also learned that Stela could not take out the same men that he had taken before that. And there was an intermission of a few days when neither I nor Vlado Fink could go to Stela's. After that, Vlado Fink never went to Stela's base to work.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Your Honour, we should go into private session for some moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, we'll go to the private session, please.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ME
utterances.text: While I was at Stela's, when Stela took me to his home, I didn't know where we were going, but then we went to his parents' for lunch, and in the car I asked him, "Was there -- what were my chances of getting released," because I wanted to go abroad and I wanted to get together with my family. And Stela said, "Don't be afraid. Nothing can happen to you. I do not have the authority to release you and take you out of Mostar, but I guarantee that nothing will happen to you, and we shall try to find some solution for you, some way to have you out." After that, I moved into the house at Dubravko Pehar's, which is right next to Stela's parents', and that is where I was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sorry. Just to clarify the situation and not to return to it: How did you leave Heliodrom on that day? Who allowed you to go from Heliodrom? Who took you from Heliodrom?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ME
utterances.text: I came out normally, like as when I went to work, with a group of prisoners. I spent a couple of nights in the base and then I moved over to that flat. I do not know how Stela explained why I wasn't coming back to work any more, why I was not at the Heliodrom.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, but you explained to the Trial Chamber that after September you were never taken to any labour outside Heliodrom.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ME
utterances.text: I don't understand the question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I just want to remind you of your testimony. Today in the courtroom, you just told that it was September that was the last month when you were involved in some sort of labour outside of Heliodrom.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ME
utterances.text: As regards that, perhaps I was returned several times. I do not remember the exact date when Stela took me to a shelter. But I know that the last time I came, I was taken out from the Heliodrom and I did not go back.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So it happened somewhere in November; right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ME
utterances.text: Yes, I suppose so. But before that, before I moved over to the flat, I slept in Stela's base for several days.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you also taken to his father's place?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ME
utterances.text: I went for lunch only once, to his father's house. I've already said that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did they take other prisoners to have lunch in his premises, I mean Stela's father?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ME
utterances.text: I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, were you ever returned to Heliodrom in September -- sorry - in December, before you were officially released from Heliodrom?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ME
utterances.text: Officially, I was not released from the Heliodrom.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: I would like the witness to be shown Exhibit 4931.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Par.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I'm not objecting. Nothing to do with the document. What I wish to say is that the time used for direct examination has already been spent, so could we please stand by our agreement that we should have a balanced ratio.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. How long are you going to take, Mr. Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Your Honour, I've got two or three questions, that's all. And I didn't object, so I didn't take your time, and you objected, you took some of my time. Sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: No. Don't calculate it in these details, Mr. Prosecutor. I'll allow you to finish that three or four questions. Then we'll break for recess.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So -- I'm sorry. Yes. The page with the last digits 7205. This is number 323. By "number," I mean the number of entry in the document. Witness, do you see your name?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ME
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When were you released, according to this entry?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ME
utterances.text: I was released - and I'm sure of it - when I last came to Stela's base. I don't know the exact date. On the 4th of December, I was in Croatia. And as for this document, Stela sent Dubravko Pehar to the SIS and said that whichever paper I bring -- I haven't brought it now, but I still have this piece of paper. It says that, the witness says his name, Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. is relieved of his term of his imprisonment and that is not the date, but another. And the man said that he knew I was a he member of the BH army and therefore he was not allowed to issue me that paper. However, I know that Pehar told me, "You know who I am and what can be done. So produce this paper, because I guarantee with my life for this man." And this paper I can send later on to the lawyers. And this date has nothing to do with it, the 3rd of December. This must have been mid-November sometime. And I have this paper. I've kept it as a personal document, as a memento

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And my next question: This is about that person who used to serve in the former Yugoslavia army and who was taken across the confrontation line with Stela's assistance. You claimed that he did not pay anything to Stela. How do you know that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ME
utterances.text: Because I was there throughout, and when the release was being discussed, Stela wasn't even in the base, because I was in the office when the man came with that former JNA officer and said that his wife and his child -- that the military police had taken his wife and child to the left bank and he was asking to be reunited with the family, so could he also be taken across. And we were together and Stela approved it. And when he said, "What can I take along?" Stela said, "Whatever you can put in four bags or sacks or something. Whatever you can carry, do it. We won't check it except weapons. You may not take any weapons." And that man waited in front of the base and Stela had already left by that time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: My question was very brief: How do you know that he did not pay? That's all. No need to explain and repeat the story again.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ME
utterances.text: He didn't pay anything in front of me, because I was present during the conversation between the two of them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know that it so happened sometimes that Vinko Martinovic did get money from Muslims for taking them across the confrontation line or taking them to some other location away from Mostar?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ME
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You did not know about it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ME
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: I would like the witness to be shown Exhibit 664.1 and distribute this document among others. I'm sorry. This issue was not in the summary of witness testimony, and that's why I have to -- had to prepare this copy just during the break.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, have you read the document?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ME
utterances.text: I have.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you give any comments to it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ME
utterances.text: Well, I can. It says here that this information has not been verified.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Your Honour, that was my last question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, we'll break here and we'll resume at 5 minutes to 6.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Mr. Par, re-examination, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very briefly, Mr. President. Re-examined by Mr. Par:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, you don't have the documents in front of you any more, so I wish to ask the usher to put before the witness the documents 601.1, which the witness has already been shown by the Prosecutor. And Mr. President, just in case I ask that we go into private session for a moment, in order to avoid revealing identities.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. We'll go into the private session, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Any questions from the Judges? Judge Clark?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. ME. I have a few questions on clarification. Questioned by the Court:

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: That latest question that was posed to you by Mr. Par, I think needs some clarification as to why a document which is dated the 28th of September should have a note at the bottom that's dated the 2nd of December, but I think that that's something that's not for you to answer. I want to go back to some other matters. You were asked a question, Mr. ME, a while ago, by the Prosecutor, when he asked you if you were a privileged prisoner. My recollection is that you responded that there was another prisoner who was more privileged, but I didn't catch his name. Now, it may be that we'll have to go into private session for that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. We'll go to the private session, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Any questions out of Judges' questions?

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Further cross-examination by Mr. Poriouvaev:

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Just one question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, answering to Judge Clark's question about the 17th of September, you stated that you were not taken to Vinko Skrobo unit; you were taken to some other unit. To which unit were you taken?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ME
utterances.text: I said, because I don't remember dates, that perhaps I was taken. I know that in the period while I was there, I was taken to Santiceva Street. That was the 2nd Battalion. And I was also taken to Malo Polje, to Buna, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: No more questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Par.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have just one question, but I would like us to go into private session, please. If we are still in private session, then it's all right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. We'll go back into the private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: [redacted].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: During the proceedings, two maps are used. One is by the Defence counsel. That is D2/31. Another is used by the Prosecutor. That is P11.18/16. They are the maps marked by the witness during the proceedings. They are admitted into evidence. Am I right, Mr. Par?

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: And as for the document P493.1, which is a new document, are you going to tender it into evidence?

utterances.speaker: MR. PORIOUVAEV
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I would like to tender it into evidence. I would also like to tender into evidence 664.1.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Any objections, Mr. Par?

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Right now I'm slightly lost with these numbers, so could you please leave me some time and I will let you know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, yes. Yes, of course. But I think that document P493.1 is just a list of the released prisoners of war.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have no objections to that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: So this document is admitted into the evidence. As for the document P664.1, I'll give you some time to consider it. So we'll have another witness. Yes. Mr. Usher, would you please bring in the next witness, please. Before I forget, I have to remind everybody: Tomorrow morning we'll move to courtroom 2 at 9.00 in the morning. Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Good evening, Witness. Can you hear me?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Would you please make the solemn declaration, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
